operations.old: Self-evolving agent skills turn execution experience into persistent instructions and code, but improved performance on the source task leaves open what has been learned. We study this question through repeated standard-task evaluations, controlled task variations, and inspection of the resulting skills and their use. Our diagnosis distinguishes source-task utility from usefulness under changes to input representation, task instances, and requirements. We examine SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills, connecting their observed reuse patterns to the decision rules preserved in their skills and the feedback used during skill construction. The results reveal different scopes of generalization despite positive source-task gains, and motivate evaluating skills by how they guide decisions when the task changes.
operations.new: Higher post-evolution scores raise an identification question: what improvement is carried by the persistent skill, and what remains useful after the task changes? We examine this question through a diagnosis of SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills, connecting their construction procedures, completed artifacts, and downstream behavior. Repeated paired evaluations establish source-task utility, controlled variations probe its scope, and skill contents and execution traces explain contrasting reuse outcomes. The evidence separates recurring benchmark gains from reusable decision guidance: positive source-task benefits coexist with sharply different responses to changed instances and requirements. Successful cases preserve criteria for selecting valid results and maintaining task constraints. This analysis connects observed gains to what the skill helps an executor decide, making behavioral persistence and attribution central to evaluating skill learning.

operations.old:
Persistent agent skills store instructions, scripts, and references that an executor can reuse across tasks. Skill-generation and evolution methods turn execution experience into these external artifacts without changing the executor's model parameters. SkillEvolver refines skills from their deployment outcomes, SPARK distills environment-verified trajectories, and CoEvoSkills jointly evolves skills and a surrogate verifier~\cite{zhang2026skillevolver,zhou2026spark,zhang2026coevoskills}. Their common goal is to make experience useful beyond the attempt that produced it.

Success on the source task does not reveal the scope of that usefulness. A skill can help by encoding a procedure that adapts to new inputs, or by preserving choices that happen to work on one instance. Both can raise a benchmark score. The distinction becomes visible when the executor must reinterpret an input, solve a replacement instance, or satisfy an additional requirement while using the same skill. These changes test what the artifact preserves from experience and what the executor must still infer.

We investigate this distinction as a diagnostic study of skill reuse. We first measure each method's gain over a same-task no-skill baseline in two standard-task runs. We then freeze the skills and examine their utility under changes to representation, instances, and requirements. Finally, we inspect contrasting examples to connect successful and unsuccessful reuse to the guidance expressed in the skills. This sequence moves from whether a skill helps to where it helps and what its contents suggest about the difference.

The resulting picture differs across methods. All three show positive paired gains in both standard-task runs. Under task variation, SkillEvolver retains positive average gains across all three change types, SPARK's gains depend on the type of change, and CoEvoSkills' average gains reverse sign. Instance changes produce the clearest separation. Thus recurring source-task gains and generalization describe different properties of an evolved skill.

The case evidence makes this distinction concrete. In signal detection, selecting a strong candidate is insufficient when the signal can be confused with background variability or a harmonic. In scheduling, a feasible output can still violate the task's repair rules. Successful reuse in these examples accompanies skills that preserve criteria for choosing and checking a result. We interpret these differences in light of the methods' feedback and skill-construction procedures.

This paper contributes a diagnosis of skill learning through three complementary forms of evidence:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Repeated utility measurement.} Six standard-task runs establish the observed paired benefits of SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills on their evaluated tasks.
    \item \textbf{Task-variation analysis.} Representation, instance, and requirement changes expose different scopes of frozen-skill usefulness across the recorded variant evaluations.
    \item \textbf{Skill-level interpretation.} Contrasting reuse examples connect outcomes to preserved decision criteria and motivate an explanation based on feedback coverage and abstraction from the source instance.
\end{itemize}
operations.new:
Agent skills externalize behavior into persistent instructions, scripts, and references that can be inspected and reused without changing model parameters. SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills construct these artifacts from execution experience through deployment-grounded revision, verified-trajectory distillation, and co-evolutionary verification~\cite{zhang2026skillevolver,zhou2026spark,zhang2026coevoskills}. A higher score after this process raises the question in our title: what has the system learned as a skill?

The final score is produced through several steps. Construction determines which guidance enters the artifact; the executor decides how to use that guidance; and a verifier assesses the resulting output. A skill can preserve a useful decision rule, an instance-specific choice, or instructions that a later executor applies incompletely. These possibilities can yield similar source-task scores while producing different behavior when the input or requirement changes. Locating the improvement therefore requires examining the persistent artifact together with its deployment.

We pursue two connected research objectives. First, we examine whether completed skills provide recurring utility and how far that utility extends under controlled task variation. Second, we investigate which decisions preserved in the skills help explain successful and failed reuse, and how those decisions relate to the feedback used during construction. This keeps the existence and scope of a benefit separate from the explanation of how it arises.

Our empirical diagnosis begins with two standard-task runs per method, pairing each skill condition with a no-skill execution of the same task. We then apply frozen skills to changes in input representation, task instances, and coupled requirements. Finally, contrasting signal-detection and scheduling cases connect the observed outcomes to the guidance used by the executor. The sequence links the score, the conditions under which it persists, and the decisions carried by the artifact.

The central finding is a separation between recurring source-task benefit and reusable behavior. All three methods have positive paired mean gains in both standard-task runs, but this agreement breaks under task variation. SkillEvolver remains positive across all three change types; SPARK and CoEvoSkills lose utility on replacement instances. The cases reveal a corresponding distinction in skill content: finding a plausible signal differs from identifying the required signal, and constructing a feasible schedule differs from preserving the rules of an acceptable repair. Successful reuse accompanies guidance that retains these distinctions.

Our contributions are an empirical diagnosis of where completed-skill utility persists, and a skill-level explanation of what successful reuse preserves. The repeated outcomes establish utility at deployment; controlled variations reveal its behavioral scope; and artifact and trace evidence connect that scope to reusable decision criteria. Together, these observations address what benchmark gains say about skill learning.

operations.new: The skill-evolution lifecycle. Construction produces a persistent artifact; deployment turns its guidance into behavior; verification assigns the observed score. We connect these stages through paired utility, frozen-skill task variation, and inspection of skill use.

\subsection{What Does an Observed Gain Identify?}

The score $V(x,A(x,s,z))$ depends jointly on the skill, its execution, and the verifier. A skill-versus-no-skill comparison measures the utility of a completed artifact at deployment. A parent-to-final comparison instead measures the change associated with revising an existing artifact. Keeping these contrasts distinct specifies which part of the learning question an evaluation answers.

Our empirical contrast is completed-skill utility. We first examine whether its paired mean is positive in each of two runs on the same task set. We then freeze the source-task skill $s_x$ and apply it to a variant $T_k(x)$, pairing its outcome with a no-skill execution on that variant. The executor can reinterpret inputs and adapt its actions; the skill itself is not revised. Persistence of utility under these changes locates the observed scope of reuse.

Attribution concerns the decisions connecting the artifact to the result. We inspect what the skill tells the executor to retain, recompute, or check, and how that guidance appears in successful and failed executions. Published construction procedures supply an explanation for how such guidance may arise. This separates observed behavior and artifact content from interpretation of the evolution pathway.

operations.new: Our study connects these evaluation levels to the identification of skill learning: repeated outcomes characterize completed-skill utility, task changes test its persistence, and skill-level examples explain the decisions behind contrasting outcomes. The unit of interpretation is the persistent artifact in use.

operations.old: We examine what self-evolving agent skills preserve through repeated standard-task evaluations, task variation, and inspection of skill reuse. SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills all yield positive source-task gains in both runs, but their variant results differ substantially. SkillEvolver has the broadest observed generalization profile, remaining positive under representation, instance, and requirement changes. SPARK's benefit depends on the change type, while CoEvoSkills' averages become negative. The inspected examples associate successful reuse with guidance for selecting valid results and preserving task-specific correctness rules. Together, these findings show why diagnosing skill learning requires examining how a frozen artifact guides behavior after the task changes.
operations.new: A higher score becomes informative about skill learning when it is connected to what the persistent artifact helps an executor do. Our repeated evaluations show positive source-task utility for all three methods, while frozen task variations separate the conditions under which that utility persists. SkillEvolver retains positive gains across the three change types; SPARK and CoEvoSkills expose narrower or adverse reuse patterns. The contrasting cases connect successful reuse to criteria for identifying valid answers and preserving repair constraints. These findings distinguish useful completed artifacts, their behavioral scope, and explanations grounded in skill content. They return the learning question to persistent decision guidance: what is retained from experience, when does it remain useful, and how does it shape the next execution?
